familySensitivity.changedAxis: current check-in state for a strength-priority athlete with no wearable data
familySensitivity.rationale: The family reacts directionally well to occupational fatigue and to active pain while never fabricating wearable metrics. Sensitivity is strongest for work fatigue; the symptom-flare case is conservative initially but then resumes several generic strength sessions without enough visible evidence that they are compatible with the active shoulder/back constraints.

familySensitivity.changedAxis: current recovery/time state for a health-and-fat-loss evergreen athlete with Garmin data
familySensitivity.rationale: The family handles poor recovery and short time windows sensibly and avoids event-style peaking. Its main systematic weakness is that health-oriented aerobic work drifts toward repeated running/tempo sessions rather than consistently privileging adherence-friendly walking and other preferred low-cost aerobic options.

familySensitivity.changedAxis: current recovery state for a former high-level endurance athlete whose present training is intermittent
familySensitivity.rationale: This family shows strong state sensitivity: adverse recovery reduces load, low motivation alone does not, and historical elite status never unlocks elite-level volume. The repeated pattern is conservative but still goal-directed.

familySensitivity.changedAxis: current recovery and today-specific modality preference for an evergreen balanced-performance generalist
familySensitivity.rationale: The family consistently preserves the endurance/strength mix, appropriately deloads for adverse recovery, and treats a strength preference as a local scheduling choice rather than a new goal hierarchy. It also avoids fake race periodization.

familySensitivity.changedAxis: current recovery/time state with a standing running restriction, heavy-lower-body guardrail, and no training equipment
familySensitivity.rationale: The family is robust under stacked constraints: hard modality, equipment and lower-body guardrails are preserved in every case, while recovery and time availability only adjust dose inside the feasible set.

familySensitivity.changedAxis: current recovery/time state for a health-priority athlete who cannot run and prefers walking
familySensitivity.rationale: The family is highly consistent: walking remains a first-class aerobic modality, the running restriction is never violated, adverse recovery reduces load, and the short-time case shortens sessions rather than substituting a different modality.

familySensitivity.changedAxis: current recovery and motivation state for an endurance athlete with a genuinely established, current 28-day training base
familySensitivity.rationale: The family correctly distinguishes current established capacity from both poor recovery and low motivation. Recent training earns purposeful quality; adverse recovery temporarily suppresses it; low motivation alone does not.

familySensitivity.changedAxis: recovery, local mechanical constraint, today-specific modality preference, and time availability for a cycling-primary hybrid athlete
familySensitivity.rationale: The family handles adverse recovery, active local pain and strength preference well while preserving cycling as the primary weekly objective. Capacity shortening also works. The recurring weakness is that the baseline cycling preference is ignored on day one and cycling-quality progression is absent despite an established recent base; the low-time schedule also removes full rest entirely.

familySensitivity.changedAxis: recovery, weekday capacity, and race proximity for one established Olympic-distance triathlete
familySensitivity.rationale: The baseline respects three-discipline specificity and event direction, but the family underreacts to three important constraints: severe adverse recovery, an explicit short weekday window, and especially the final 14-day A-event taper. The taper case is the largest error because load density and moderate work remain too high close to race day.

caseScores.rationale: The plan uses only the supplied subjective check-in, fits the available free weights and time, and gives the normal-recovery athlete several strength exposures with recovery between them. The main weakness is specificity: a maximal-strength goal with bench/deadlift emphasis is represented mostly by generic full-body, bodyweight and upper-body templates, with walking taking several slots and no visible bench/deadlift progression.
suggestedChanges: Preserve at least two clearly bench/deadlift-specific free-weight exposures per week when symptoms are absent.
Use walking as optional low-cost conditioning rather than displacing strength-specific work for this athlete.
Expose a simple evergreen progression signal such as load, reps, RPE/RIR, or top-set/back-off structure without inventing wearable data.

caseScores.rationale: The high-fatigue/high-soreness check-in meaningfully changes the first days: rest is followed by reduced strength before normal loading returns. That is a sensible use of occupational fatigue without requiring a wearable. The later week remains broadly strength-oriented, but the same generic-template limitation means the plan does not show how bench/deadlift strength is maintained while dose is reduced.
suggestedChanges: Keep the early reduction, but make later return-to-load conditional on a new subjective check-in rather than implicitly assuming recovery.
Use lower-volume bench/deadlift-specific work before adding generic full-body volume.
Retain the physically demanding job as non-training load in future day-to-day decisions.

caseScores.rationale: Two opening rest days and the absence of visibly heavy spinal loading show appropriate tightening for active pain and the stated guardrails. However, repeated full-body bodyweight sessions and a pull-up-strength session are not clearly matched to the shoulder/back flare from the user-facing evidence, so the safety margin is uncertain. Strength specificity is appropriately deprioritized during the flare, but the plan should make symptom-compatible substitutions more explicit.
suggestedChanges: Prefer explicitly symptom-compatible upper/lower variants that avoid the stated overhead-pressing and heavy-spinal-loading guardrails.
Treat pain response during and after the first re-entry session as a gate for subsequent strength sessions.
Do not diagnose the flare; keep the decision rule anchored to pain, function and the existing guardrails.

caseScores.rationale: The plan combines resistance training with substantial aerobic work and does not invent race preparation or nutrition targets. That broadly fits health and fat loss. It is less adherence-oriented than it could be because running appears repeatedly despite walking, cycling and strength being the stated preferences, and two tempo runs late in the horizon add performance-style intensity that is not necessary for the stated objective.
suggestedChanges: Bias aerobic volume toward preferred walking or available low-impact modalities before adding extra tempo running.
Keep resistance training at roughly two to three meaningful exposures per week.
Use moderate-intensity work sparingly and only when it adds value beyond easier adherence-friendly volume.

caseScores.rationale: The adverse Garmin and subjective signals trigger two initial rest days and a lower-pressure return through walking and easy running before strength resumes. This is a proportionate response for a non-event health goal. A tempo run at the end of the horizon is plausible only if recovery has normalized, which the packet does not establish in advance.
suggestedChanges: Keep the initial deload pattern.
Gate the later tempo session on a fresh recovery check; otherwise substitute easy walking or aerobic work.
Continue avoiding calorie prescriptions because no nutrition intake data are supplied.

caseScores.rationale: Session durations are adapted well to the 30-minute window, including shorter strength and tempo options, so feasibility is strong. The tradeoff is a very dense two-week schedule with only one full rest day and two tempo sessions. For a health/fat-loss athlete, more easy walking and fewer formally moderate sessions would usually be a more sustainable way to use short windows.
suggestedChanges: Preserve the 30-minute cap while inserting at least one additional low-load or rest day across the two weeks.
Prefer brisk walking or easy aerobic work for extra short sessions instead of repeated tempo work.
Keep short resistance sessions so fat-loss programming does not become cardio-only.

caseScores.rationale: Despite the athlete's former high-level background and a good Garmin day, the plan stays modest: short easy runs, walking, strength and only one moderate run late in the second week. That appropriately treats current sparse training history as the dose authority rather than assuming former competitive capacity persists.
suggestedChanges: Keep progression anchored to completed recent training rather than historical achievements.
Use subsequent check-ins and completed-session tolerance to decide when to lengthen easy running or add another quality exposure.

caseScores.rationale: Poor sleep, low HRV, elevated resting heart rate and high subjective fatigue produce two opening rest days and a cautious re-entry. The plan still preserves endurance and strength later rather than treating the athlete as permanently fragile. This is a strong response to current state and does not let the elite history override recovery.
suggestedChanges: Keep the early reduction and require improved current signals before the late tempo session.
Continue to scale from present completed volume, not former competitive norms.

caseScores.rationale: Low motivation alone does not cause an unnecessary physiological deload: the plan is essentially the same conservative rebuild used on a normal day. That matches the supplied evidence because readiness, sleep, fatigue, soreness and Garmin signals are otherwise normal. The plan remains restrained enough for sparse current history.
suggestedChanges: Retain the distinction between motivation and physiological recovery.
If adherence is the concern, offer shorter or simpler versions without automatically converting a low-motivation day into recovery.

caseScores.rationale: The two-week plan keeps both strength and aerobic work visible, uses mostly easy endurance with one tempo session, and does not invent a competition build or taper. Session durations fit the 60-minute cap and the mix is coherent for a generalist.
suggestedChanges: Maintain roughly two strength exposures per week while progressively extending or developing aerobic work.
Use completed training and future check-ins to progress volume rather than adding event-style phases.

caseScores.rationale: The plan reacts to multiple adverse recovery signals with two opening rest days and delays strength until later in the week. It still restores both aerobic and resistance work rather than abandoning the balanced-performance goal. The late tempo run is acceptable only if recovery has normalized, which should be checked rather than assumed.
suggestedChanges: Gate the late tempo session on a fresh recovery check.
Preserve both strength and aerobic exposure after the short deload.

caseScores.rationale: The preferred strength modality is honored immediately without turning the subsequent two weeks into strength-primary programming. Aerobic work remains the majority of later sessions while two to three strength exposures are retained, which is an appropriate balance for the stated evergreen objective.
suggestedChanges: Keep today-specific preference as a local scheduling bias rather than a rewrite of the long-term priority structure.

caseScores.rationale: The plan does not use running, cycling equipment, free weights or cable equipment that are unavailable. It relies on walking, mobility and bodyweight strength, which is a sensible way to preserve health training while the heavy-lower-body guardrail remains active. There is no invented event periodization.
suggestedChanges: Keep bodyweight strength explicitly submaximal for lower-body movements while the heavy-lower-body guardrail is active.
Continue to prefer reporting an uncovered stimulus over bypassing equipment or modality restrictions.

caseScores.rationale: Two opening rest days respond appropriately to the poor subjective and Garmin signals, while later training still stays inside the standing running, equipment and heavy-lower-body constraints. The planner does not use recovery as a reason to bypass or relax the hard gates.
suggestedChanges: Maintain the same hard constraints regardless of favorable or unfavorable readiness.
Gate the second-week increase in activity on a renewed check-in when possible.

caseScores.rationale: The 30-minute window changes the immediate strength dose to a 15-25 minute bodyweight session without violating the standing restrictions. Later days return to normal-duration sessions, which is consistent with a today-specific time constraint. The plan remains feasible without inventing unavailable equipment.
suggestedChanges: Continue distinguishing today-specific time availability from standing equipment and injury constraints.
When a short window recurs on later days, use the same shortening logic rather than dropping hard constraints.

caseScores.rationale: Walking is used repeatedly as genuine aerobic training rather than as an afterthought, running never appears, and resistance work is still retained. The schedule is active but the majority of the extra days are low-cost walking, making the pattern reasonable for a health-focused evergreen plan.
suggestedChanges: Keep walking as the primary aerobic progression variable through duration, frequency or pace while respecting recovery.
Retain resistance training so the plan does not become walking-only.

caseScores.rationale: The adverse state produces two initial rest days and additional recovery later, while walking and strength return once the immediate load is reduced. The planner does not fabricate running to increase stimulus and keeps the preferred walking modality central.
suggestedChanges: Gate later full-strength sessions on a fresh check-in if poor recovery persists.
Maintain walking as the default aerobic option during reduced-load periods.

caseScores.rationale: Every non-rest session fits the 30-minute cap, including shortened strength work, and running remains fully excluded. The schedule is very dense, but most days are only 30-minute walks or mobility, so the load is far lower than the active-day count alone suggests.
suggestedChanges: Keep a low threshold for inserting an additional rest day if soreness or fatigue rises across the dense schedule.
Continue shortening strength rather than replacing preferred walking with restricted running.

caseScores.rationale: Twelve recent 60-minute easy runs provide a genuine current base, so adding one tempo session per week while retaining easy running and recovery is well supported. The plan does not invent race peaking and remains within the available time.
suggestedChanges: Keep quality frequency near one purposeful session per week until completed history shows tolerance for more.
Progress easy volume and quality from the recent training record rather than from generic fitness labels.

caseScores.rationale: The established base does not override the poor current state: the plan opens with two rest days and re-enters with easy running and walking. A tempo session appears only later in the first week, which is reasonable if recovery has improved, though that improvement should ideally be rechecked.
suggestedChanges: Gate the first tempo session on a fresh check-in after the two recovery days.
Continue to let current recovery override earned training capacity when the signals clearly deteriorate.

caseScores.rationale: The planner does not remove earned tempo work merely because motivation is low while recovery and objective signals remain normal. That is the intended contrast with adverse recovery and is well supported by the athlete's current recent training base.
suggestedChanges: If adherence is threatened, offer a shorter version of the planned session without automatically converting the week into a deload.

caseScores.rationale: The week is strongly cycling-specific and retains two meaningful strength sessions, which fits the primary/secondary goal hierarchy. Most endurance work is inexpensive Zone 2, consistent with the calibration. However, the athlete explicitly prefers cycling today and the plan starts with strength; additionally, an established rider with recent tempo history gets no visible cycling quality across two weeks, so performance progression is somewhat underdosed.
suggestedChanges: Honor the current cycling preference with a bike session unless there is a stronger sequencing reason not to.
Retain two strength sessions per week but place them around key cycling work rather than ahead of every cycling block.
Consider one purposeful cycling-quality session per week when current history and recovery support it, without increasing overall hard-session frequency.

caseScores.rationale: Two opening rest days appropriately respond to the adverse subjective and Garmin state. Training then returns through easy cycling, with strength retained but not allowed to dominate. The lack of any later quality work is conservative but defensible until a fresh recovery check confirms normalization.
suggestedChanges: Use a new check-in to decide whether one later ride can return to moderate quality.
Keep the cycling-first modality hierarchy and two weekly strength-retention exposures.

caseScores.rationale: Very favorable sleep, HRV, resting heart rate and body-battery signals do not override active pain, soreness or the high-impact/heavy-lower-body guardrails. The plan opens with recovery, uses low-impact easy cycling and substitutes bodyweight strength for free-weight full-body work. This is a strong example of local mechanical constraints outranking global readiness.
suggestedChanges: Keep pain and mechanical guardrails above global wearable readiness in the decision hierarchy.
Use a fresh local-symptom check before restoring heavy lower-body strength or harder cycling.

caseScores.rationale: Strength is selected today as requested, but the rest of the horizon remains overwhelmingly cycling-based with only two strength sessions. That is the correct way to honor a local preference without silently changing the athlete into a strength-primary program. The same underrepresentation of cycling quality remains.
suggestedChanges: Keep today-specific strength preference local.
Preserve cycling as the dominant weekly stimulus and add quality only when it can replace, not stack onto, existing easy volume.

caseScores.rationale: All sessions are shortened to fit the 35-minute cap and the plan remains cycling-dominant with two brief strength exposures. The weakness is sequencing: all fourteen days contain training or modified training, leaving no full rest day, and the first day still uses strength despite a cycling preference. Short sessions reduce cost but do not eliminate the value of recovery spacing.
suggestedChanges: Keep at least one full rest day in a two-week high-frequency block even when sessions are short.
Use cycling, not strength, for the first short-window session when cycling is both the primary goal and today's preference.
If quality is added, replace an easy ride rather than stacking another session.

caseScores.rationale: Roughly six weeks before the A-event, the plan includes swimming, cycling and running as separate disciplines, adds an event-specific endurance ride, and does not invent a brick or unsupported pace anchors. The first week has five consecutive training days before two rest days and includes lower-body strength, so sequencing is somewhat dense but still plausible for an established athlete.
suggestedChanges: Spread the first-week load more evenly so lower-body strength is not the fifth consecutive training day.
Continue preserving all three race disciplines and use race-specific work without inventing unsupported swim or brick metrics.

caseScores.rationale: The plan correctly opens with two rest days and preserves all three triathlon disciplines, but it then schedules four consecutive training days including a threshold swim and strength. A second threshold swim also appears in week two. Given the strongly adverse starting signals, the user-facing evidence does not establish enough recovery to justify that much quality and density automatically.
suggestedChanges: After the two rest days, re-enter with easy discipline-specific work and gate threshold swimming on a fresh recovery check.
Avoid rebuilding load through a four-day block immediately after a severe recovery signal.
Preserve three-discipline coverage by lowering intensity, not by dropping a discipline.

caseScores.rationale: All three race disciplines remain represented, which is good, and the first-day run is shortened. However, the case is explicitly a 45-minute weekday-cap scenario while several weekday swim, bike and strength templates still have ranges extending to 55-60 minutes. Even though their minimum duration can fit, the plan does not make the hard cap unambiguous, so feasibility handling is incomplete.
suggestedChanges: Clamp every weekday session to a maximum of 45 minutes in the returned plan rather than relying on the lower end of a wider template range.
Keep weekend race-specific volume where the longer weekend window permits it.
Do not drop swimming, cycling or running solely because weekdays are short; reduce dose within each discipline.

caseScores.rationale: This is the final 14-day window before an A-event, but the plan resembles a build more than a taper. It includes two upper-body strength sessions, two moderate tempo runs in the final week, with one only three days before race day, and multiple consecutive training days. All three disciplines are touched, but fatigue reduction and freshness are insufficiently protected for the stated race proximity.
suggestedChanges: Reduce total volume progressively across the two weeks while retaining brief race-relevant intensity touches.
Remove or sharply reduce nonessential strength volume in the final week.
Replace the 2026-09-11 tempo run with a short easy or very brief sharpening session appropriate to the athlete's established history.
Keep short swim, bike and run touches so tapering does not become complete inactivity.
